prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, showing how trade reallocates resources across firms and shapes aggregate productivity and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: I keep B010 as a single-part prize to Helpman and Melitz. My laureates and alternatives are unchanged from round 1. I have tightened the citation wording after Fredriksson's and Enflo's points. The core is Melitz (2003) together with Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple. It replaced the representative-firm industry with heterogeneous firms. It explains who exports and why liberalisation reallocates activity towards more productive firms. It also adds a selection channel to the gains from trade. The framework has had more than twenty years of testing on firm-level data from many countries, and it is standard in trade, macro and industrial organisation. The credit is a clean two-person line, and each name is tied to a specific, citable body of work. Corporate finance is my field, so I come to this with a contracting and data-and-theory sensibility: a model that organises firm-level facts and makes testable predictions about who is affected by a change in the environment. B010 does that well. The first-round tally is 3-3-3-2 across four candidates. I do not treat it as evidence of merit, and I do not move toward any position to create a majority. Having read the exchange, I still find B010 the most defensible on attribution, maturity and durability of the mechanism. I regard B014, B032 and B016 as serious cases, and B010 is not clearly ahead of them on scientific grounds.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is the uncredited lineage. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum developed closely related heterogeneous-firm models and the exporter-premia facts, and none of them is on this ballot. A Helpman-Melitz prize therefore cuts through a larger body of ideas, and the citation must be worded to avoid implying that these two own all of it. The second reservation is quantitative. Welfare gains from selection depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity, and the sufficient-statistics results suggest they may be smaller than first claimed. The prize would then honour a mechanism and a framework, not a settled magnitude. Third, Krugman's 2008 prize covers adjacent ground. I read the heterogeneity-within-industry strand as distinct, but a reasonable member could read it as partly incremental. Fourth, other trade candidates outside the shortlist (B003, B041) and Helpman's role in them could divide the Committee's view of how to recognise the field. Finally, B010 is not obviously stronger than B014 or B032 on influence outside trade. B014 has a much larger footprint in policy practice, and B032 has more transparent identification. My preference rests on attribution cleanliness and on maturity combined with durability of the mechanism, and I accept that others may weigh breadth of consequence more heavily.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B010 second and treats Melitz and Helpman as foundational. He warns that quantitative work suggests smaller welfare gains from selection than first claimed, and that Bernard, Eaton and Kortum could be seen as co-originators. He also notes that Helpman appears in several trade candidacies, which could split support.
responses.response: I accept the size-of-gains and co-origination points as real. I would not let them decide the matter, for three reasons. The exporter premia and within-industry reallocation are firm-level facts that survive a modest welfare effect. The reassessment of the size of the gains is itself conducted in the framework's language. And the Committee can only credit names on the ballot, so the Bernard et al. lineage belongs in the background documentation and in the citation's scope. On split support, I do not think the existence of other trade candidacies counts against B010's attribution. Helpman's credit on this ballot rests on specific work, Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus foreign direct investment. I also take your wider point seriously. B014's policy footprint is larger than B010's. My difference with you is how much weight breadth of consequence should get against the clarity of the credit line, and I do not claim to have settled that.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg ranks B032 first and B010 fifth. She argues that B010's quantitative welfare gains depend more on functional-form choices, such as the Pareto assumption, than the transparent reduced-form designs in B032 do. She concedes that this is a judgement and not a decisive scientific difference.
responses.response: I agree that the functional-form dependence is the sharpest quantitative critique of B010, and it is my main substantive worry as well. I draw a different conclusion about what the prize would honour. The citation I propose rests on the selection and reallocation mechanism and the firm-level facts it organises, not on a welfare number. In B032 the qualitative finding of persistent local costs is also stronger than the aggregate magnitude. So both candidates are more secure on mechanism than on magnitude. Your replication-and-re-examination criterion is one I value. For B010, more than twenty years of firm-level evidence across many countries is the nearest equivalent, though it is less cleanly design-based than the local labour-market evidence. I would also like to know what specific re-examinations of shift-share inference and persistence you rely on, since the chair has asked B032 supporters this and it would help me compare the two on equal terms.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B010 with Helpman and Melitz. He argues that, because the Bernard et al. empirical facts are uncredited, the citation should be about the theoretical framework of firm heterogeneity and selection and should not claim discovery of exporter premia as such. He also keeps Redding out as a separable later strand.
responses.response: I accept this wording constraint and have applied it. My round-1 citation said the work explains exporter selection, and I have replaced it with a version that speaks of incorporating heterogeneity and selection into trade theory and of how trade reallocates resources. It does not claim to have discovered the exporter premia. I also agree on Redding. His quantitative and spatial work is later and more separable. Adding a third name would make the credit line less clean, and I do not see an attribution gain from it. We differ slightly on emphasis. You say your opinion does not rest on trade expertise. I am in the same position, as corporate finance is my field. So I would not claim priority judgements in the trade literature beyond what the documented papers and colleagues' accounts support.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B010 seventh. He says the credit boundary with Bernard, Eaton and Kortum and the quantitative-trade literature is contested, and that competing claims within trade mean this strand may not be the one recognised. As chair he also asks what would move members to another candidate.
responses.response: I take the credit-boundary point as the strongest argument against my preferred part, and I answer it directly. If the Committee finds that excluding Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum makes a Helpman-Melitz prize indefensible, then B010 should fall behind a candidate with a cleaner credit line. I would then move to B042, whose Kiyotaki-Moore attribution is tight, or to B016 if the identification caveats are written into the citation. The same standard applies to my own preference. I withdrew B006 for attribution reasons after your argument about Vishny, and the principle is unchanged. I do not think the existence of competing trade claims by itself defeats B010. The question is which strand of trade can be credited most cleanly from names on the shortlist, and I still think that is B010, though I hold it as a judgement and not as a fact.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B010 first but holds it somewhat less firmly than in her opening because of B032's broad support. She would describe the contribution as selection and reallocation without a magnitude claim. She regards trade as a field that the Committee may recognise only once.
responses.response: I agree on the wording and on the two-person cut. I would add that her reason for softening her preference, B032's breadth of opening support, is not something I count as merit. If she softens it for attribution or identification reasons, I would want to hear them. On the once-only point, I share the concern that the Committee may recognise trade only once, and that is why the choice of strand matters. I still think B010 is the strand with the best-defined listed credit set, as she argued against Hassler. Where I am less certain than she is, is how much the Committee will care about the missing Bernard et al. names compared with B032's missing Acemoglu-Restrepo and Levy-Murnane credit. These are comparable attribution gaps, and I do not see a principled reason to treat one as disqualifying and the other as acceptable.

uncertainties: Whether the uncredited Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum lineage makes a Helpman-Melitz prize incomplete in a way that the citation wording cannot repair, which is the point on which my preference is most exposed.

How much the quantitative welfare-gains debate (Pareto productivity, sufficient-statistics results) should affect the way the achievement is characterised. I can describe the mechanism without a magnitude, but I am not sure all members would accept that.
Whether Redding should be a third name, or whether his quantitative and spatial work is a separable later contribution. I treat it as separable.
How to compare B010 with B014 and B032 on breadth of consequence versus attribution cleanliness. I have not resolved this to my own satisfaction, and I do not think vote counts can resolve it.
Whether B010 or a different trade strand (B003, B041, outside the shortlist) is the better way to recognise the field, if the Committee recognises trade at all.

My views on trade, law and finance, and political economy rest on my own recollection of the literature and on colleagues' stated accounts, not on independent source verification. Prior-prize facts are members' recollections as well.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship, institutional tie or other connection to Helpman or Melitz appears in the supplied profile. The same applies to the B016 names (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) and the B042 names (Moore, Kiyotaki, Gertler). My principal co-author, Steven Kaplan, and my other documented co-authors are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I disclose my adjunct appointment at Chicago Booth, my long overlap on the Committee with Hassler, Krusell, Ellingsen and Svensson, and my position as Vice President of the Academy. None involves a credited candidate. My field is corporate finance, which is closest to B006. I withdrew that candidate on attribution grounds, and I treat proximity to it as a possible bias. I also note that SSE colleagues (Andersson, Dreber Almenberg, Friberg) sit on the committee. These are disclosures, not adjudicated conflicts.
